title: Finn and the Wobbly Stairs
markdown:
Every school has a special something, and Oakhaven School’s was not the wonky hall clock, nor the lopsided gingerbread man on Mrs. Gable’s desk that always looked as if it had stubbed a toe. It was the staircase.

It was Finn’s staircase. Finn the stairkeeper. Not a keeper of keys or secrets, but of steps. The stairs were grand polished oak, and they had opinions. They stretched and shrank, twisted and turned, on a timetable known mainly to themselves. Finn’s job was to see that everyone arrived, even when “where they were going” changed every five minutes.

His friend Whisper, a stair sprite no bigger than a robin, flitted with wings like moonlight caught in a dewdrop. “Finn, my dear fellow,” she would chirrup, bells in a breeze. “Another morning for the Oakhaven Oscillations. Are the steps feeling springy?”

They were. At the first bell a thump-wobble-jiggle ran through the building, as familiar as turning pages. The grand stair, which usually climbed from dusty ground to cheerful first floor, might whoosh toward the art room instead, paintings beckoning like a dare.

Finn would sigh, sandy hair ruffled, and guide the children with his trusty, slightly squeaky mop. “Mind the sway, little ones. Hold on. This way to history.”

“This way to adventure,” Whisper would correct, a dragonfly of giggles.

One Tuesday the third bell chimed for lessons, and the staircase began its usual jig. This time it did not finish. It wobbled with extra vigour and stopped halfway, top landing smack against the attic observatory door. The climbers went poof into the school’s pockets: some in dusty broom cupboards, some behind forgotten gym mats, a whole class of Year Fours in the stationery cupboard among reams of paper and boxes of pencils, having an impromptu lesson on rubbers.

“Oh dear,” Finn whispered. His brow crumpled like a map left in a pocket. This was a bigger jiggle than the everyday kind.

The intercom cleared its throat like a grumpy badger. Mrs. Prickleworthy, the Headteacher, sounded like a kettle that had forgotten how to whistle. “Attention. Due to an unexpected structural anomaly with our main staircase, all classes will proceed with extreme caution. Finn, Mr. Finn, report to my office immediately.”

Finn and Whisper were already on the moving stair, stranded halfway to nowhere. Going down might mean missing the only chance to help. The usual path had vanished into the school’s peculiar architecture.

His knees considered becoming jelly left in the sun. Above them the tiny round attic door seemed a distant star in a sky of plaster and beams. A tremor ran to the mop. Too high, said a small trapped-bird thought. Palms clammy.

“We have to get to the attic,” Whisper said, firm as a little drum. She zipped before his nose. “That’s where the Great Gear is. It decides the final landing. If we set it right, everyone comes free.”

He looked at the steep slide of oak. The ground floor, currently theoretical, would have been easier. He pictured Year Fours giggling among the paper, pale faces in broom dark. “All right,” he said, dust in the breath. “For them.”

The first brave step changed the feel of the thing. The sway grew less sway-like. The steepness remembered manners. He watched Whisper, the mission, the idea of relieved faces. The tummy-butterflies folded a wing.

Halfway up, the oak remembered it was a slide and tried to be one. Finn planted the mop, then thought better of trusting a mop on a slope, and used his hands. Whisper flew the next three steps as a banner. Below, a Year Four sneezed in the stationery cupboard, which meant at least one child was still breathing paper-scent and not panic. That sneeze put another inch of height into Finn’s legs.

They reached the door. Finn shoved. Inside, a huge whirring of gears and levers hummed like a mechanical giant after lunch. Brass, iron, shiny cogs: the Great Gear, heart of the stair’s magic. Dust hung in the attic light like extra punctuation. A skylight showed a slice of ordinary Tuesday sky, which felt like a kindness.

“Quick,” Whisper urged. “Turn it to Settled. Tell the stairs to be still.”

His hands shook, but purpose had arrived. He left the squeaky mop on a dusty ledge to get a better grip, grasped the largest lever, cool and smooth, and pulled until a clunk travelled the attic. Outside, the staircase gave a last gentle shudder, a cat stretching, and lay down in its proper place, ground floor to first, as if it had only been joking. The old building seemed to sigh.

The attic door burst. Mrs. Prickleworthy stood in sensible shoes, relief and bewilderment sharing her face. “Finn. Whisper. What in the name of all that is orderly are you doing up here? And why is the main staircase behaving so… cooperatively?”

She looked out. The stair was itself again. Children peeked from cupboards and mats and began to cheer, a happy wave down the newly honest steps.

Finn stood taller. The butterflies had clocked off. A warm glow, sunshine on a chilly landing, took their place. He even managed a small confident smile.

“We just made sure everything was settled, Headteacher.”

Whisper winked from his shoulder. “That’s the curious thing about stairkeepers. They put things in the right place, even when the place is a bit wobbly.”

The relieved children poured down, laughter finding the halls. A little step ahead gave a tiny, almost private shimmy. Finn, without thinking, steadied it with a calm hand. He looked at the oak, then at Whisper, a knowing twinkle ready for the next oscillation. Mind the sway, the school seemed to say. He was already minding it.
